      REPLY BRIEF OF JOINT CO-LOCATION DEVELOPERS AND MOTION TO
     INTERVENE OUT-OF-TIME OF CALIBRANT, CONVERGENT, U.S. ENERGY
                    STORAGE COALITION, AND VERRUS

        Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (Commission) December 18,

2025 order (Co-Location Order),1 Eolian, L.P. (Eolian), Antora Energy, Inc., Calibrant Energy

(Calibrant), Convergent Energy and Power (Convergent), Mainspring Energy, Inc. (Mainspring),

U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, and Verrus, LLC (Verrus) (collectively, the Joint Co-Location

Developers) submit this response to the Initial Briefs filed by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM)

and the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (PJM TOs) on February 23, 2026. Pursuant to Rule

214 of the Commission Rules of Practice and Procedure,2 Calibrant, Convergent, U.S. Energy

Storage Coalition, and Verrus also submit a motion to intervene out-of-time. The brief is

supported by the affidavit of Andrew Levitt and Aniruddh Mohan of the Brattle Group on behalf

of Eolian, at Attachment A.3

        The Joint Co-location Developers believe in the promise of the Co-Location Order and

would like to pursue business models based on the new services offered. We are deeply

concerned, however, that PJM’s proposed transmission service provisions will render the new

 transmission services commercially unworkable. We urge the Commission to require PJM to

adopt transmission service terms that deliver on the promise of the Co-Location Order and

enable customers to meet their commercial needs through co-location arrangements.

        The Commission issued the Co-Location Order within the context of a broader national

effort to confront the affordability, reliability, and speed-to-power challenges that rapid large load

growth poses for the electricity system. The Co-Location Order promises to cut through those

challenges by requiring PJM to make common-sense reforms, allowing Eligible Customers to

take new “transmission services that reflect their actual impact on the transmission system” and

thereby “avoid costly and inefficient transmission system buildout that may not be necessary.”4

As Commissioner Rosner summarized, the Commission’s goal was “to meet surging demand

while upholding two fundamental values that underpin the electric industry in our country: first,

that all customers have a right to receive electric service on a timely basis, and second, that

electric service should be reliable and affordable for all customers.”5

        The proposals in PJM’s Initial Brief fall short of fulfilling that promise. PJM departs from

the requirements and spirit of the Co-Location Order again and again, rendering the new

transmission services commercially unworkable. PJM’s response to the Commission’s demand

for bold leadership largely amounts to a continuation of the “business-as-usual approach to load

growth—planning for generation and load separately.”6 This “will not suffice to timely meet

growing demand while also keeping prices reasonable.”7 PJM’s proposal would do little to

improve reliability, avoid unnecessary infrastructure, and enable timely interconnection.

        The Commission should reject PJM’s proposal and direct a replacement rate that delivers

on the Co-Location Order’s promise. Most importantly, the Commission should direct PJM and

the PJM TOs, as applicable, to make the following changes:

          •   Make Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service (CDS) available as
              needed during normal operations, as the Co-Location Order required, rather than
              only during a generator outage, as PJM has proposed.

          •   Clarify that a Co-Located Load receiving Interim Network Integration
              Transmission Service (NITS) can take energy from its co-located generator during
              curtailment conditions.

          •   Clarify when and how Non-Firm CDS and Interim NITS will be curtailed.

          •   Clarify that charging of energy storage resources does not require transmission
              service, whether or not such resources are stand-alone resources or are part of a
              co-location configuration together with Co-Located Load, and as such charging of
              co-located storage does not apply toward customers a Non-Firm CDS customer’s
              Maximum Facility Output limitation.

          •   Offer a rate for Non-Firm CDS that reflects cost causation principles.

          •   Modify PJM’s draconian penalty proposal. Penalties are appropriate where a
              customer fails to respond to PJM’s curtailment instructions in a manner consistent
              with its service obligations. But penalties must balance the need to deter conduct
              that is harmful to the system with the need to limit excessive and unnecessary
              costs.

          •   Given the urgent need to address the impacts of load growth on the PJM system
              today, the Commission should require PJM to make the new tariff provisions
              related to the new transmission services effective sooner than June 1, 2029.

 I.     JOINT CO-LOCATION DEVELOPERS’ INTEREST IN THE PROCEEDING
AND MOTION TO INTERVENE OUT-OF-TIME OF CALIBRANT, CONVERGENT,
U.S. STORAGE COALITION, AND VERRUS

          Eolian develops energy generation and storage assets throughout the United States and

has originated 27 GW of operating capacity to date. Eolian and its partners have developed

projects supporting large loads in multiple regions across the United States, including PJM.

Eolian expects to develop storage or generation assets co-located with loads.

          Antora is a U.S. manufacturer of thermal batteries, which are domestically built in San

Jose, California, and developer of thermal storage projects for industrial facilities in the U.S. and

abroad.

          Calibrant develops energy generation and storage assets throughout the United States.

Calibrant and its partners have developed and expect to continue to develop projects in PJM

through a range of configurations, including behind-the-meter generation (BTMG) and co-

located projects supporting large loads. Specifically, Calibrant has several existing BTMG

projects and projects that are currently being developed worth millions of dollars that could be

impacted by PJM’s proposed transmission service framework.

          Convergent develops, owns, and operates distributed energy storage and storage plus

solar resources for large commercial, industrial, and utility customers across North American

markets, including PJM. Convergent has resources in operation and in development in PJM

including behind-the-meter distribution and transmission connected battery energy storage

systems, front-of-the-meter distribution connected battery energy storage systems, both with and

without attached solar systems, and a 20 MW flywheel resource in Hazleton, Pennsylvania.

          Mainspring is a U.S.-headquartered manufacturer of modular, fuel-flexible, and

dispatchable linear generators, a new type of power generator. Mainspring was founded in 2010




                                                  4
 and its first commercial units were deployed in 2020. The company has been rapidly scaling

since 2023, deploying its innovative technology across a wide spectrum of customer types and

use cases. The company’s customers include investor-owned utilities, public power utilities,

municipal water treatment facilities, biogas facilities, data centers, grocery store chains, cold

food storage, and hospital systems. Mainspring’s linear generators can be installed behind a

customer’s utility meter or as a front of the meter grid asset. Mainspring linear generators are

currently operating across multiple sites in PJM territory and are in development across

additional sites.

        The U.S. Energy Storage Coalition unites America’s leading grid battery manufacturers,

energy storage developers, owners, and operators. The U.S. Energy Storage Coalition advances

policies and solutions to ensure grid reliability amidst historic demand for power, lower energy

costs for all Americans, strengthen grid capacity to support new industrial and AI infrastructure,

and rapidly scale American manufacturing and minerals production.

        Verrus is a developer, owner, and operator of a first-of-its-kind fleet of purpose-built,

load-flexible hyperscale data centers. Verrus designs facilities from the ground up to function not

only as digital infrastructure but also as grid assets—a new class of large customer capable of

dynamically adjusting electricity consumption to support reliability, efficiency, and affordability.

Verrus’ facilities can provide these system benefits without disrupting the critical computing

workloads that increasingly underpin the modern economy. Each Verrus campus integrates on-

site utility-scale battery energy storage, advanced load-management controls, and grid-aware

automation that collectively enable real-time coordination with utilities and regional transmission

operators.




                                                  5
          Joint Co-Location Developers therefore have a substantial interest in this proceeding that

cannot be adequately represented by another party. The concerns that Joint Co-Location

Developers raise will critically support development of Co-Located Loads and storage assets that

avoid “costly and inefficient transmission system buildout.”8 Their participation is therefore in

the public interest.

         The Commission granted Eolian’s, Antora’s, and Mainspring’s motions to intervene at the

show cause stage of this proceeding.9 Calibrant, Convergent, U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, and

Verrus, however, move to intervene out-of-time for the first time here. These parties respectfully

request that the Commission grant this request to intervene out-of-time.10 The posture of this

proceeding has changed significantly with the Commission’s initiation of the paper hearing

proceeding in a way that has crystalized these parties’ interest. These parties accept the record as

it stands, and this intervention will not place any additional burden on any other party, nor will it

disrupt or delay Commission proceedings in this matter, because the same brief is submitted by

Eolian, Antora, and Mainspring, even absent these additional parties’ intervention.

II.      ARGUMENT

         A.    The Co-Location Order requires that Non-Firm CDS be available as needed
         during normal operations, not solely when a generator is on outage, as PJM has
         proposed.

         PJM proposes to limit the availability of Non-Firm CDS to “the event the Co-Located

Generating Facility is on outage and unable to provide any of the dedicated level of energy.”11

But the Co-Location Order made clear that Non-Firm CDS is to be available for reservation by

The Commission offered the scenario of a generator outage as an example of when an Eligible

Customer might use Non-Firm CDS.13 But this was clearly just an example, not a limitation on

the availability of the service. The Commission intended the service to function in a manner

“similar to existing non-firm transmission service options in the Tariff,”14 which contain no such

limitation.

        Even if the Co-Location Order were unclear (which it is not), PJM has not offered an

adequate rationale for limiting the availability of Non-Firm CDS to periods of generator

outages.15 References to the “complexity” of providing Non-Firm CDS cannot overcome the

benefits that Non-Firm CDS will create for PJM ratepayers and large load customers seeking

timely interconnection.

                 1.       PJM’s proposal is commercially unworkable.

        As the Commission explained, the availability of Non-Firm CDS allows co-located

resources that can control their withdrawals from the grid to interconnect in a manner that avoids

unnecessary network upgrades and unnecessary procurement of capacity.16 Were PJM to follow

through on the Commission’s order as drafted, it would enable a business model that has the

potential to benefit ratepayers by increasing grid utilization while reducing or avoiding the cost

of new infrastructure. Ensuring that Non-Firm CDS is available during non-emergency operating

interconnection to meet the loads’ needs based on grid economics, including the relative scarcity

of energy during peak conditions as well as transmission congestion. While the large load

customers would be responsible for ensuring that they have ample assets and load flexibility to

curtail as necessary given potential constraints, the ability to rely on the system for significant

periods of time would provide critical service necessary to reliably meet the load’s demand at

reasonable cost while promoting the efficient utilization of existing transmission infrastructure

consistent with economic dispatch and real-time system conditions.

        PJM’s approach would instead require inefficient system operations. Limiting the

availability of Non-Firm CDS will undermine economic efficiency by preventing Co-Located

Loads from using grid power at times when wholesale energy prices are lower than the marginal

cost of the co-located generator. Under PJM’s approach, a customer taking Non-Firm CDS

would be required to dispatch on-site generation even during periods when LMP is negative.

        Use of as-available Non-Firm CDS would also allow a load relying on thermal resources

to significantly decrease the number of starts required, considerably reducing reliability risks, as

well as operations and maintenance needs.17 Ability to take non-firm service during non-

emergency conditions is particularly critical to cost-effectively leveraging energy storage

resources to serve the load, as Non-Firm CDS must be able to support load while storage is held

in reserve for peak periods, is depleted, or is charging.18

                                                         8
          This same dynamic holds true for other strategies a load customer may use to reduce

reliance on the grid during critical periods, such as by modulating load. PJM’s proposed

approach allows for no market-based response based on customers’ willingness to hold risk. In

the Commission’s approach, by combining Non-Firm CDS with Firm CDS, customers may seek

full redundancy with generation at the point of interconnection, no redundancy, or anywhere in

between and tolerate curtailment risk up to the individual customer’s appetite. In PJM’s proposed

approach, customers are bound to a specific level of redundancy, which will restrict competition

and innovation.

         In addition, PJM’s approach may inadvertently threaten reliability for other customers.

PJM’s proposal to restrict Non-firm CDS to times when the co-located generator is on outage

appears to be tailored to baseload resources. Given that it takes many years to develop new

baseload resources, PJM’s proposal, to the extent it is workable at all, is most likely to be used

by existing baseload resources (such as nuclear plants and gas-fired combined cycles), who may

exit the market and enter into co-located arrangements with loads taking Non-Firm CDS.19

         Finally, PJM’s filing is unclear whether customers may take Non-Firm CDS during

partial outages.20 PJM’s brief states that a customer could take service “up to the MW level that

the Co-Located Generating Facility is on outage,” suggesting that perhaps a partial outage is

permissible.21 However, the illustrative tariff appears to require an all-or-nothing approach. The

illustrative tariff indicates that Non-Firm CDS is available when the co-located generator is

intends the illustrative tariff language to control, it should address the perverse incentives created

by that rule, including the fact that this structure would encourage co-located generators to

                 2.       PJM’s approach is not necessary to maintain system reliability.

        Restricting Non-Firm CDS to periods of generator outage is also unnecessary to maintain

system reliability. To the contrary, PJM’s Interim NITS proposal demonstrates PJM’s ability to

offer interruptible, non-firm service during normal conditions without the need to request

reservation.23 Instead, rendering this service commercially unworkable will make it harder for

new customers to connect to the system without overwhelming the grid. By stymying a Non-

Firm CDS model that would encourage loads to bring their own capacity and reduce reliance on

PJM system capacity, PJM’s approach would result in more loads following the status quo model

that has strained PJM’s capacity market. Further, PJM’s approach could even prevent such loads

from dispatching up when doing so would help to address a reliability challenge, such as when

increasing consumption could mitigate a potential thermal overload on a transmission facility, or

absorb excess reactive power to address high voltage conditions. In providing a service

framework for dispatchable loads, PJM should leverage the capabilities of these loads to ensure

system reliability. Given the fact that grid operators across the globe reliably count on energy

storage resources to follow dispatch instructions, PJM does not adequately explain its reticence

to rely on similarly-dispatchable loads.

          We recommend that, in studying a request for Non-Firm CDS, PJM model the precise

characteristics of the load and co-located generation, accounting for their proximity to one

another, and appropriately accounting for generator outage and RAS or SPS contingencies.24

Such studies should model the load as dispatchable, examining transmission system limits and

identifying transmission system conditions when Non-Firm CDS will not be made available.25

Those studies would impose limits on the use of Non-Firm CDS, but those limits need not be

nearly so restrictive as the proposed limit to periods when the co-located generator is on outage.

Rather, any operation restrictions would flow from system constraints. As discussed further

below, similar to the study process it uses in providing for provisional interconnection service to

generators, PJM can and should update such studies periodically, so as to ensure that such

operating limits remain up to date.26

         PJM’s position on Non-Firm CDS also does not square with its other service offerings.

PJM already offers non-firm point-to-point service that is reservable whether or not the load has

co-located generation, and whether or not any such generation is on outage. Like non-firm

transmission service, Non-Firm CDS should be offered on an as-available basis, to be reserved

on an hourly, daily, or (rolling) monthly basis. Further, PJM plans to offer non-firm Interim NITS

on an as-available basis, demonstrating that it can provide for a reliable service framework that

provides non-firm service during normal operating conditions.27

         If anything, Non-Firm CDS can more readily be offered during normal conditions than

Interim NITS, because the service structure behind Non-Firm CDS allows for day-ahead

reservation. As discussed in the affidavit of Levitt et al., Non-Firm CDS is granted based on both

studies for interconnection, and day-ahead reservation review by PJM.28 Under this structure,

PJM could provide for Non-Firm CDS to be available during normal operating conditions

subject to any reservation limits identified in the interconnection study, while denying

reservations to the extent that its day-ahead predictions demonstrate a particular hour (or day) to

approach transmission system limits.29

        Any SPS or RAS would operate only after these mechanisms are put in place, to ensure

that the load does not show up on the grid unexpectedly. For example, PJM’s Matthew Wharton

provides that “PJM would expect the RAS to actuate on the loss of the Co-Located Generating

Facility” such that “the load served by Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service or

Interim NITS will automatically be removed from the system by the RAS scheme.”30 Thus,

while SPS and RAS “should not be installed as a substitute for good system design or operating

practices,”31 that would not be the case here were PJM to enable Non-Firm CDS across a broader

range of circumstances. As with other services, RAS or SPS would operate only as a fail-safe

backup after PJM’s planning measures and dispatch process provide for curtailment to the extent

the transmission system is constrained.

Instead, PJM should update the operating conditions framework for Non-Firm CDS periodically

be the first line of defense in ensuring PJM’s reliability, we note that RASs can operate reliably

        B.     PJM should clarify that its transmission service requirements for energy
        storage charging apply equally to storage co-located with load, and exempt
        customers from the Maximum Facility Output where the customer’s load shape and
        characteristics are inherently flexible.

        PJM studies the charging of energy storage resources through its generator

interconnection process.37 It does not require energy storage resources to take transmission

service for charging, except where the storage charges during the zonal peak hour without being

dispatched.38 As applied here in conjunction with the Maximum Facility Output (MFO)

PJM has taken in response to stakeholder questions,40 this service framework appears to allow

the relevant Co-Located Load to take service while the co-located energy storage resource

the generator is at least 100% of the non-firm load size).”42

          As applied to co-location configurations involving energy storage resources, this rationale

only holds true to the extent that PJM clarifies (1) that charging of the co-located energy storage

resource can take place without taking transmission service,43 and (2) that the limit is measured

by the resource’s nameplate capacity.44 As Andrew Levitt and Anirrudh Mohan explain, PJM

should clarify that “even if a co-located facility has 0 MW of Firm CDS and 0 MW of Non-Firm

CDS, a co-located storage component that has been granted an Interconnection Service

Agreement recognizing its ability to withdraw from the grid for charging may still do so as

dispatched by PJM, consistent with a standalone storage facility.”45

         Further, even with this clarification, PJM’s MFO limit should also not apply to inherently

flexible loads that operate at low load factors, such as thermal energy storage. Such loads would

not anticipate taking transmission service on an 8760 basis like many other large loads (thermal

energy storage can provide 24/7 thermal output with a load factor of only 33%) and instead

would plan to charge only when prices are very low at the point of delivery, because generation

from low or zero marginal cost generators exceeds local demand.46 To the extent PJM is

concerned that variable transmission usage above MFO would create unmanageable scheduling
